claim: TRP proteins are a large family of cation-selective channels, surpassed in variety only by voltage-gated potassium channels.
source: Transient receptor potential (TRP) proteins are a large family of cation-selective channels, surpassed in variety only by voltage-gated potassium channels.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract without direct experimental data in this manuscript, but represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Changes in TRP channel function and expression are associated with a variety of metabolic, respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurological diseases.
source: Changes in TRP channel function and expression are associated with a variety of metabolic, respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurological diseases (Nilius et al., 2007; Nelson et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The abnormal expression of TRP channels has been related to cancer development and progression.
source: Moreover, the abnormal expression of TRP channels has been related to cancer development and progression (Shapovalov et al., 2016; Yang and Kim, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPs have been shown to be evolutionarily related to all voltage-gated cation channels (VGCCs), two-pore channels (TPCs or TPCNs), and CatSper channels.
source: TRPs have been shown to be evolutionarily related to all voltage-gated cation channels (VGCCs), two-pore channels (TPCs or TPCNs), and CatSper channels (Yu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The TRP family is composed of two major groups (Groups I and II) and 10 subfamilies: TRPA1, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPC, TRPM, TRPS, TRPN, TRPY/TRPF PKD2s, and TRPML.
source: The TRP family is composed of two major groups (Groups I and II) and 10 subfamilies, or subtypes: TRPA1, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPC, TRPM, TRPS, TRPN, TRPY/TRPF PKD2s, and TRPML (Ramsey et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Group I (GI) gathers members of TRPC, TRPM, TRPS, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPA, and TRPN subfamilies.
source: While Group I (GI) gathers members of TRPC, TRPM, TRPS, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPA, and TRPN subfamilies; Group II (GII) is composed of members of the TRPML, PKD2, and TRPY/TRPF channels (Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007; Himmel and Cox, 2020; Himmel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Group II (GII) is composed of members of the TRPML, PKD2, and TRPY/TRPF channels.
source: While Group I (GI) gathers members of TRPC, TRPM, TRPS, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPA, and TRPN subfamilies; Group II (GII) is composed of members of the TRPML, PKD2, and TRPY/TRPF channels (Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007; Himmel and Cox, 2020; Himmel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRP channels share poor cation selectivity and a loose sequence similarity.
source: In general, TRP channels share poor cation selectivity and a loose sequence similarity (Ramsey et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TRP channels have the ability to integrate multiple stimuli (e.g., chemical, mechanical, electrical, and thermal) to promote channel opening.
source: Cataloged as polymodal ion channels, they have the ability to integrate multiple stimuli (e.g., chemical, mechanical, electrical, and thermal) to promote channel opening.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about TRP channels.

claim: The polymodality observed in TRPs has been explained in terms of allosteric interactions.
source: Such polymodality observed in TRPs has been explained in terms of allosteric interactions (Brauchi et al., 2004; Latorre et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Different sensor modules in TRP channels couple to each other and to the channel pore, modulating permeation.
source: Different lines of research have shown that the different sensor modules couple to each other and to the channel pore, modulating permeation (Hui et al., 2003; Castillo et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRP channels share the general architecture of voltage-gated ion channels (VGICs).
source: Structural data revealed that TRP channels share the general architecture of voltage-gated ion channels (VGICs) (Kasimova et al., 2016; Cheng, 2018; Cao, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRP channels assemble as domain-swapped tetramers, with monomers containing six transmembrane segments (i.e., TM1–TM6) flanked by cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal domains.
source: They assemble as domain-swapped tetramers, with monomers containing six transmembrane segments (i.e., TM1–TM6) flanked by cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal domains.
evidence: This represents established structural knowledge about TRP channels.

claim: The transmembrane helices TM5 and TM6, together with the section between them, give shape to the conductive pore.
source: The transmembrane helices TM5 and TM6, together with the section between them, give shape to the conductive pore (Ramsey et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The first four transmembrane helices (TM1–TM4) and the intracellular domains have been described as regulatory regions as they provide binding sites for agonists and cofactors.
source: The first four transmembrane helices (TM1–TM4) and the intracellular domains have been described as regulatory regions as they provide binding sites for agonists and cofactors (Steinberg et al., 2014; Voolstra and Huber, 2014; Cao, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The TM1 and TM4 transmembrane region shows fundamental differences with known VGICs, where the absence of charged residues within the transmembrane region should be underscored.
source: The TM1 and TM4 transmembrane region shows fundamental differences with known VGICs, where the absence of charged residues within the transmembrane region should be underscored (Palovcak et al., 2015; Cao, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPMs and TRPVs are about tenfold less voltage-dependent compared to voltage-gated potassium channels.
source: It has been shown that TRPMs and TRPVs are about tenfold less voltage-dependent compared to voltage-gated potassium channels.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The modest voltage dependence observed in TRP channels is likely supported by residues located in the pore region.
source: The modest voltage dependence observed in TRP channels is likely supported by residues located in the pore region (Liu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The TM1 and TM4 transmembrane region hosts binding pockets for ligands in all the different TRP channel subtypes, serving as a ligand-binding domain (LBD) in TRPs.
source: The TM1 and TM4 transmembrane region hosts binding pockets for ligands in all the different TRP channel subtypes, serving as a ligand-binding domain (LBD) in TRPs (Steinberg et al., 2014; Huffer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The phylogenetic hypothesis presented in this study is well supported and resolves the sister group relationships among the main groups of TRP channels.
source: In our case, the proposed phylogenetic hypothesis is well supported and resolves the sister group relationships among the main groups of TRP channels.
evidence: This is a claim about the results of the phylogenetic analysis performed in this study.

claim: The monophyly of the TRP gene family was recovered with strong support of 98%.
source: We not only recovered the monophyly (i.e., the single evolutionary origin of the TRP gene family) with strong support of 98%, but also the diversity of TRP channels into two main groups: (1) GI-TRPs, a clade containing TRPA1, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPC, TRPGamma, TRPN1, TRPY/TRPF, TRPM, and TRPS channels; and (2) GII-TRPs, a clade containing PKD2 and MCLN channels (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The diversity of TRP channels is divided into two main groups: (1) GI-TRPs, containing TRPA1, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPC, TRPGamma, TRPN1, TRPY/TRPF, TRPM, and TRPS channels; and (2) GII-TRPs, containing PKD2 and MCLN channels.
source: We not only recovered the monophyly (i.e., the single evolutionary origin of the TRP gene family) with strong support of 98%, but also the diversity of TRP channels into two main groups: (1) GI-TRPs, a clade containing TRPA1, TRPV, TRPVL, TRPC, TRPGamma, TRPN1, TRPY/TRPF, TRPM, and TRPS channels; and (2) GII-TRPs, a clade containing PKD2 and MCLN channels (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Four well-supported clades for GI-TRPs were recovered: (A) TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1, (B) TRPC/TRPGamma/TRPN1, (C) TRPY/TRPF, and (D) TRPM/TRPS.
source: We recovered four well-supported clades for GI-TRPs: (A) TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1, (B) TRPC/TRPGamma/TRPN1, (C) TRPY/TRPF, and (D) TRPM/TRPS.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The sister group relationship between the TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1 and TRPC/TRPGamma/TRPN1 clades was recovered with strong support.
source: Among these, we recovered the sister group relationship between the TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1 and TRPC/TRPGamma/TRPN1 clades with strong support (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The TRPY/TRPF group was recovered sister to the TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1 and TRPC/TRPGamma/TRPN1 clades.
source: Moreover, the TRPY/TRPF group was recovered sister to the latter (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The TRPM/TRPS clade was recovered sister to all other members of GI-TRPs.
source: The TRPM/TRPS clade was recovered sister to all other members of GI-TRPs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: A TRP sequence from Coccomyxa subellipsoidea was recovered sister to the TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1 clade.
source: According to our analyses, a TRP sequence from Coccomyxa subellipsoidea was recovered sister to the TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1 clade, while a TRP sequence from C. reinhardtii was recovered sister to the TRPM/TRPS clade (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: A TRP sequence from C. reinhardtii was recovered sister to the TRPM/TRPS clade.
source: According to our analyses, a TRP sequence from Coccomyxa subellipsoidea was recovered sister to the TRPV/TRPVL/TRPA1 clade, while a TRP sequence from C. reinhardtii was recovered sister to the TRPM/TRPS clade (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: All other TRP sequences from unicellular organisms considered in this work are more evolutionarily related to the GII-TRP clade.
source: As reported before (Arias-Darraz et al., 2015), all other TRP sequences from unicellular organisms considered in this work are more evolutionarily related to the GII-TRP clade (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and is also supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TM regions are well defined and conserved in TRP channels.
source: In agreement with previous structural alignment studies (Huffer et al., 2020), we observed that TM regions are well defined and conserved (Figure 2a).
evidence: This observation is based on the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2a and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Gaps detected in the alignment are mostly confined to linkers in between TM segments.
source: Moreover, we observed that gaps detected in the alignment are mostly confined to linkers in between TM segments.
evidence: This is an observation from the multiple sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Gaps are almost non-existent at the intracellular linker between TM4 and TM5, the elbow connecting TM6 with the TDh, and the TDh itself.
source: In contrast, gaps are almost non-existent at the intracellular linker between TM4 and TM5, the elbow connecting TM6 with the TDh, and the TDh itself (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is an observation from the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The pattern of gaps in the loops connecting transmembrane segments seems to be a good predictor for the subfamily grouping.
source: The pattern of these gaps in the loops connecting transmembrane segments seems to be a good predictor for the subfamily grouping (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The longer linker between preTM1 and TM1 is characteristic of TRPM channels.
source: This is the case of the longer linker between preTM1 and TM1 that is characteristic of TRPM channels, or the extended TM3–TM4 loop seen in channels from the TRPC family (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extended TM3–TM4 loop is seen in channels from the TRPC family.
source: This is the case of the longer linker between preTM1 and TM1 that is characteristic of TRPM channels, or the extended TM3–TM4 loop seen in channels from the TRPC family (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRPV, TRPC, and TRPN channels display a larger linker between TM5 and the selectivity filter/pore helix.
source: While TRPV, TRPC, and TRPN channels display a larger linker between TM5 and the selectivity filter/pore helix, TRPMs show a larger linker region between the selectivity filter/pore helix and TM6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRPMs show a larger linker region between the selectivity filter/pore helix and TM6.
source: While TRPV, TRPC, and TRPN channels display a larger linker between TM5 and the selectivity filter/pore helix, TRPMs show a larger linker region between the selectivity filter/pore helix and TM6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A discrete set of highly conserved residues (identity>90%) common to the TRP superfamily was identified.
source: A thorough analysis of the distribution of amino acids identified a discrete set of highly conserved residues (identity>90%) common to the TRP superfamily (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: About 69% of TRP channels analyzed have 12 conserved and non-contiguous amino acids interpreted as an amino acid signature or fingerprint (W F Φ G Φ Φ Φ N L I A W; where Φ could be either Phe or Tyr).
source: About 69% of TRP channels analyzed have 12 conserved and non-contiguous amino acids we interpreted as an amino acid signature or fingerprint (W F Φ G Φ Φ Φ N L I A W; where Φ could be either Phe or Tyr; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: 95% of the TRP channels contained at least nine of the conserved side chains in the fingerprint.
source: We observed that 95% of the TRP channels contained at least nine of these conserved side chains (Figure 2c; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis shown in Figure 2c and Table 1.

claim: The bacterial potassium channel KvAP displays five conserved residues in relatively similar positions to the TRP fingerprint.
source: In contrast, the bacterial potassium channel KvAP displays five conserved residues in relatively similar positions while Kv1.2 exhibits only three (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison shown in Table 1.

claim: Kv1.2 exhibits only three conserved residues in relatively similar positions to the TRP fingerprint.
source: In contrast, the bacterial potassium channel KvAP displays five conserved residues in relatively similar positions while Kv1.2 exhibits only three (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison shown in Table 1.

claim: TRPVs, TRPCs, and TRPMs conserve the complete set of 12 fingerprint residues (W F Φ G Φ F Φ N L I A W).
source: While TRPVs, TRPCs, and TRPMs conserve the complete set of 12 residues (W F Φ G Φ F Φ N L I A W), TRPNs show 11 (W F Y G Φ Y Φ N L V A W), TRPA1 10 (W F Y G F F F N L I G R), and the more distantly related TRPY only 8 residues.

claim: TRPNs show 11 fingerprint residues (W F Y G Φ Y Φ N L V A W).
source: While TRPVs, TRPCs, and TRPMs conserve the complete set of 12 residues (W F Φ G Φ F Φ N L I A W), TRPNs show 11 (W F Y G Φ Y Φ N L V A W), TRPA1 10 (W F Y G F F F N L I G R), and the more distantly related TRPY only 8 residues.
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison.

claim: TRPA1 shows 10 fingerprint residues (W F Y G F F F N L I G R).
source: While TRPVs, TRPCs, and TRPMs conserve the complete set of 12 residues (W F Φ G Φ F Φ N L I A W), TRPNs show 11 (W F Y G Φ Y Φ N L V A W), TRPA1 10 (W F Y G F F F N L I G R), and the more distantly related TRPY only 8 residues.
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison.

claim: TRPY shows only 8 fingerprint residues.
source: While TRPVs, TRPCs, and TRPMs conserve the complete set of 12 residues (W F Φ G Φ F Φ N L I A W), TRPNs show 11 (W F Y G Φ Y Φ N L V A W), TRPA1 10 (W F Y G F F F N L I G R), and the more distantly related TRPY only 8 residues.
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison.

claim: The differences observed in TRPA1 can be mapped to the TDh.
source: The differences observed in TRPA1 can be mapped to the TDh.
evidence: This is an observation from the sequence analysis.

claim: The TDh is considered an important modulator of TRP gating.
source: The latter is considered an important modulator of TRP gating and although different in sequence in TRPA1 channels when compared to other GI-TRPs, it is structurally equivalent (Paulsen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The TDh in TRPA1 channels is structurally equivalent to that in other GI-TRPs, although different in sequence.
source: The latter is considered an important modulator of TRP gating and although different in sequence in TRPA1 channels when compared to other GI-TRPs, it is structurally equivalent (Paulsen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The specific specialization in TRPA originated after the divergence from the common ancestor shared with TRPVs and is unlikely to be found outside this group.
source: Thus, our results suggest that such specific specialization in TRPA originated after the divergence from the common ancestor shared with TRPVs and is unlikely to be found outside this group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic and sequence analysis results.

source: Within the unicellular algae set crTRP1, which shares a common ancestor with the TRPM family, shows only seven fingerprint residues that increases up to nine for the case of csTRP2 that shares a common ancestor with the clade containing TRPV, TRPVL, and TRPA1 channels (Figure 2c; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison shown in Figure 2c and Table 1.

claim: csTRP2 shows nine fingerprint residues.
source: Within the unicellular algae set crTRP1, which shares a common ancestor with the TRPM family, shows only seven fingerprint residues that increases up to nine for the case of csTRP2 that shares a common ancestor with the clade containing TRPV, TRPVL, and TRPA1 channels (Figure 2c; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison shown in Figure 2c and Table 1.

claim: A highly conserved glycine (86.3%) is commonly found at the selectivity filter.
source: These include a highly conserved glycine (86.3%) commonly found at the selectivity filter, a phenylalanine (85.5%) at the beginning segment of TM5, and an aspartic acid (85,2%) localized at the end of TM4–TM5 linker.

claim: A highly conserved phenylalanine (85.5%) is found at the beginning segment of TM5.
source: These include a highly conserved glycine (86.3%) commonly found at the selectivity filter, a phenylalanine (85.5%) at the beginning segment of TM5, and an aspartic acid (85,2%) localized at the end of TM4–TM5 linker.
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis.

claim: A highly conserved aspartic acid (85.2%) is localized at the end of TM4–TM5 linker.
source: These include a highly conserved glycine (86.3%) commonly found at the selectivity filter, a phenylalanine (85.5%) at the beginning segment of TM5, and an aspartic acid (85,2%) localized at the end of TM4–TM5 linker.
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis.

claim: The phenylalanine at the beginning of TM5 and the aspartic acid at the end of TM4–TM5 linker are in close proximity to L678 (according to rTRPV1 numbering), a sidechain associated to channel response to both agonist and pH in different TRPs channels.
source: The latter two residues are in close proximity to L678 (according to rTRPV1 numbering) a sidechain associated to channel response to both agonist and pH in different TRPs channels (Boukalova et al., 2010; Du et al., 2009; Kasimova et al., 2017; Klausen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from the sequence analysis, supported by citations to previous literature.

source: These results were corroborated by a hidden Markov model (HMM) analysis using the same dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: All three identified TPCs are thought to be asymmetric.
source: All three identified TPCs are thought to be asymmetric (Penny et al., 2016; Kintzer and Stroud, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: One domain (D1) of TPC shows six coincidences with the TRP fingerprint.
source: In support of the argument of asymmetry, while one domain (D1) shows six coincidences with the TRP fingerprint, the other domain (D2) is more similar to eukaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) with only five coincidences (Table 1).

claim: The other domain (D2) of TPC is more similar to eukaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) with only five coincidences with the TRP fingerprint.
source: In support of the argument of asymmetry, while one domain (D1) shows six coincidences with the TRP fingerprint, the other domain (D2) is more similar to eukaryotic voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) with only five coincidences (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison shown in Table 1.

claim: The monomeric bacterial channel NabAB shares seven of the eleven signature residues with the TRP fingerprint.
source: Interestingly, the monomeric bacterial channel NabAB (Payandeh et al., 2011) shares seven of these eleven signature residues, and the mammalian Nav1.4 exhibits only five of these residues in domain III, which holds the highest number of hits compared to other domains (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence comparison shown in Table 1, with citation to the structure of NabAB.

claim: The mammalian Nav1.4 exhibits only five of the signature residues in domain III, which holds the highest number of hits compared to other domains.
source: Interestingly, the monomeric bacterial channel NabAB (Payandeh et al., 2011) shares seven of these eleven signature residues, and the mammalian Nav1.4 exhibits only five of these residues in domain III, which holds the highest number of hits compared to other domains (Table 1).

claim: TPC and bacterial Nav channels exhibit the larger score of conservation at the fingerprint outside the TRP family.
source: Thus, in our analysis, TPC and bacterial Nav channels exhibit the larger score of conservation at the fingerprint outside the TRP family.

claim: Phylogenetic and primary sequence analyses provide strong support for a fingerprint in GI-TRP channels that is composed of 7–11 non-contiguous residues (W F Φ G Φ Φ Φ N L I A W).
source: Overall, phylogenetic and primary sequence analyses provide strong support for a fingerprint in GI-TRP channels that is composed of 7–11 non-contiguous residues (W F Φ G Φ Φ Φ N L I A W).

claim: Three well-defined clusters (patches) of fingerprint residues are present in representative channels of the different families, including crTRP1 from green algae.
source: By doing this structural mapping, we identified three well-defined clusters (hereafter referred to as patches) of fingerprint residues that are present in representative channels of the different families, including crTRP1 from green algae (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The sequence alignments are in full agreement with reported structural alignments.
source: By extending our structural alignment to match with recently published results (Huffer et al., 2020), we not only confirmed that our sequence alignments are in full agreement with reported structural alignments, but we observed that the three-dimensional arrangement of the fingerprint is a robust feature among TRPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a validation of the sequence alignment results by comparison with published structural alignments, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The three-dimensional arrangement of the fingerprint is a robust feature among TRPs.
source: By extending our structural alignment to match with recently published results (Huffer et al., 2020), we not only confirmed that our sequence alignments are in full agreement with reported structural alignments, but we observed that the three-dimensional arrangement of the fingerprint is a robust feature among TRPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first patch (P1) is composed of side chains from pre-TM1 (Trp426 [95.3%]), the TM1 (Phe434 [95.5%]), the TM4–TM5 linker (Gly563 [98.0%]), and the TDh (Trp697 [93.1%]).
source: The first patch (P1) gathers several residues from a hotspot that has been historically linked to channel modulation. It is composed of side chains from pre-TM1 (Trp426 [95.3%]), the TM1 (Phe434 [95.5%]), the TM4–TM5 linker (Gly563 [98.0%]), and the TDh (Trp697 [93.1%]) (Figure 3b; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the structural and sequence analysis shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claim: Glycine 563 at the linker and Tryptophane 697 at the TDh have been reported as a common theme in TRPs.
source: Initially proposed as critical for TRPV1 channel activation (Gregorio-Teruel et al., 2014), Glycine 563 at the linker and Tryptophane 697 at the TDh have been reported as a common theme in TRPs (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and summarized in Table 2.

claim: The TDh seems to operate as an integrator between various functional elements, receiving information from lipids (such as PIP2), the TM4–TM5 linker reporting changes occurring at the transmembrane region, and the coupling domain (CD) composed of the pre-TM1 helix and a helix-loop-helix (HLH) motif.
source: In this context, the TDh seems to operate as an integrator between various functional elements, receiving information from lipids (such as PIP2), the TM4–TM5 linker reporting changes occurring at the transmembrane region, and the coupling domain (CD) composed of the pre-TM1 helix and a helix-loop-helix (HLH) motif.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural analysis and previous knowledge.

claim: The CD in TRPs is thought to participate in the functional association between the cytosolic and the transmembrane domain.
source: This CD in TRPs is thought to participate in the functional association between the cytosolic and the transmembrane domain.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about TRP channels.

claim: The high conservation of Phe434 is underscored by the importance of the CD array that integrates with critical cytoplasmic features.
source: The high conservation of Phe434 is underscored by the importance of the CD array that integrates with critical cytoplasmic features (Garcia-Elias et al., 2015; Romero-Romero et al., 2017; Hofmann et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2018; Hilton et al., 2019; Yuan, 2019; Zubcevic et al., 2019; Cao, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The second patch (P2) is located at the selectivity filter region and is composed of three phenyl group residues: Phe591 [Φ 96.6%], Phe638 [Φ 96.8%], and Tyr666 [Φ 98.6%], located at both the TM6 helix and the pore helix.
source: The second patch (P2) is located at the selectivity filter region and is composed of three phenyl group residues, that is, Phe591 [Φ 96.6%], Phe638 [Φ 96.8%], and Tyr666 [Φ 98.6%], located at both the TM6 helix and the pore helix (Figure 3b; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the structural and sequence analysis shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claim: The high conservation of the three phenyl residues located within the selectivity filter and pore helix contrasts with the otherwise high variability observed in this region (i.e., turret and re-entry linker).
source: The high conservation of these three phenyl residues located within the selectivity filter and pore helix contrasts with the otherwise high variability observed in this region (i.e., turret and re-entry linker) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: A third patch (P3) is localized at the lower portion of the pore and is composed of a well-studied set of residues forming the lower gate (Asn676 [93.7%], Ile679 [89.7%], and Ala680 [95.3%]) as well as Leu678 [95.3%] that is facing the interface between TM5 and TM6.
source: A third patch (P3) is localized at the lower portion of the pore and is composed of a well-studied set of residues forming the lower gate (Asn676 [93.7%], Ile679 [89.7%], and Ala680 [95.3%]) as well as Leu678 [95.3%] that is facing the interface between TM5 and TM6 (Palovcak et al., 2015; Figure 3b; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the structural and sequence analysis shown in Figure 3b and Table 1, with citation to previous literature.

claim: A prevalent aromatic side chain (Tyr441 [76.5% Tyr+14.4% Phe]) is located at the middle of the TM1 helix.
source: Finally, we identified a prevalent aromatic side chain (Tyr441 [76.5% Tyr+14.4% Phe]), located at the middle of the TM1 helix (Figure 3b; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claim: Mutations at position Tyr441 have been reported deleterious for TRPV1 channel function.
source: Mutations in that position have been reported deleterious for TRPV1 channel function (Boukalova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Tyr441 was not observed in close proximity to any other fingerprint residue.
source: This residue was not observed in close proximity to any other fingerprint residue (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 3b and c.

claim: The most conserved interaction among fingerprint residues is between the Gly563 at the TM4–TM5 linker and Trp697 at the TDh.
source: From the structural data, the most conserved interaction among fingerprint residues is between the Gly563 at the TM4–TM5 linker and Trp697 at the TDh.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: Evolutionary coupling analysis (ECA) shows that the highest score for putative interactions is between the TM4–TM5 linker and the TDh.
source: This observation is further supported by our evolutionary coupling analysis (ECA), showing that the highest score for putative interactions is precisely those established between the TM4–TM5 linker and the TDh (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the evolutionary coupling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: ECA links the lower portion of TM2 to the end of the TDh.
source: ECA also links the lower portion of TM2 to the end of the TDh.
evidence: This is a result from the evolutionary coupling analysis.

claim: The high covariance score between TM2 and the TDh could involve an additional linker molecule such as PIP2 or other lipid binding to this region.
source: Structurally, such interaction cannot be easily explained by direct contact between residues from TM2 and TDh. Thus, it follows that the high covariance score between TM2 and the TDh could involve an additional linker molecule such as PIP2 or other lipid binding to this region (Poblete et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2018; Yazici et al., 2021; Hughes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and evolutionary coupling analysis, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interactions between the channel and membrane lipids at the cytosol-membrane interface are emerging as a common theme in TRPs.
source: Interactions between the channel and membrane lipids at the cytosol-membrane interface are emerging as a common theme in TRPs.
evidence: This represents emerging knowledge in the field.

claim: Different parts of the CD/TDh coupling mechanism are tuned by the differences in binding of membrane lipids and/or canonical ligands.
source: Under this view, different parts of the CD/TDh coupling mechanism are tuned by the differences in binding of membrane lipids and/or canonical ligands (reviewed in Zubcevic, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Mutations of residues that form part of the fingerprint—or the connecting side chains—modify or impair channel activity.
source: Series of independent studies had reported that mutations of residues that form part of the fingerprint—or the connecting side chains—modify or impair channel activity, underscoring their importance in maintaining proper channel activity (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by a summary of previous studies in Table 2.

claim: Mean distance between fingerprint residues of the same patch is low, suggesting proximity as observed in the exemplary structures.
source: Mean distance between fingerprint residues of the same patch is low, suggesting proximity as observed in the exemplary structures (Figure 3c and d; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 3c, d, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The normalized variance of pairwise distances between fingerprint residues on each patch is low, suggesting that fingerprint residues on each patch remain in close proximity with each other, regardless of the variation in conformations rendered during experimental derivation.
source: Moreover, the normalized variance of these pairwise distances is also low (Figure 3e, purple squares). This suggests that fingerprint residues on each patch remain in close proximity with each other, regardless of the variation in conformations rendered during experimental derivation.
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Sections of high pairwise variability are detected, such as pre-TM1, where the variance is higher for the distances with the linkers TM2–TM3 and TM4–TM5.
source: In contrast, sections of high pairwise variability are also detected. This is the case of pre-TM1, where the variance is higher for the distances with the linkers TM2–TM3 and TM4–TM5 (Figure 3e, darker regions).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The lower gate transition to the open state involves the motion of the lower portion of the TM6.
source: As reported abundantly in literature, the lower gate transition to the open state involves the motion of the lower portion of the TM6 (Susankova et al., 2007; Salazar García et al., 2009; Cao et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Large variability of distances between TM5 and TM6 is observed, an indication of the multiple conformations included in the statistical analysis.
source: Accordingly, we can observe the large variability of distances between TM5 and TM6, an indication of the multiple conformations we included in our statistical analysis (Figure 3e, darker regions).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The TM1–TM4 region displays larger variability among close residues.
source: Moreover, the TM1–TM4 region displays larger variability among close residues (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The amino acids belonging to the different patches are consistently close to regions of larger variability.
source: Notably, the amino acids belonging to the different patches are consistently close to regions of larger variability (Figure 3e; dark spots next to purple squares).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Four phenyl groups (i.e., Phe/Tyr) were identified in specific positions within the transmembrane domain in more than 90% of the sequences.
source: Four phenyl groups (i.e., Phe/Tyr) were identified in specific positions within the transmembrane domain in more than 90% of the sequences (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: These residues are part of a larger cluster of aromatic residues facing the center of the four-helix bundle formed by TM1–TM4, that are common to all TRP channel structures.
source: Further inspection of structural data showed that these residues are part of a larger cluster of aromatic residues facing the center of the four-helix bundle formed by TM1–TM4, that are common to all TRP channel structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: A group of five to eight inward-facing aromatic residues belonging to the LBD domain (including at least one signature residue from P1), appear to form an aromatic core (AC).
source: A group of five to eight inward-facing aromatic residues belonging to the LBD domain (including at least one signature residue from P1), appear to form an AC (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Voltage-gated potassium and sodium channels occupy these positions with charged amino acids forming salt bridges, short aliphatic side chains, or aromatics located at the membrane-water interface.
source: In contrast, voltage-gated potassium and sodium channels occupy these positions with charged amino acids forming salt bridges, short aliphatic side chains, or aromatics located at the membrane-water interface (Figure 4a; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural comparison shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The aromatic core (AC) is present in all TRP subtypes, connecting three to four helices from within the LBD, suggesting they could serve as a scaffold that stitches together the whole domain.
source: Although the overall three-dimensional shape of the AC varies (Figure 4c), it is present in all TRP subtypes, connecting three to four helices from within the LBD, suggesting they could serve as a scaffold that stitches together the whole domain.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4c, with an inference about function.

claim: The putative AC emerges as a common theme present from crTRP1 to TRPV1–4.
source: This putative AC emerges as a common theme present from crTRP1 to TRPV1–4 (Figure 4b; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TRPV1–4 clade exhibits both the highest number of aromatics (8) and the most ordered stack.
source: The most dramatic case is observed in the TRPV1–4 clade, exhibiting both the highest number of aromatics (8) and the most ordered stack (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is a result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: TRPA1 shows only five aromatics forming the AC without a clear stacking.
source: On the other hand, TRPA1 shows only five aromatics forming the AC without a clear stacking, as observed also in the other subfamilies (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Although the residues in TRPA1 are still in close contact, they do not form the compact stacking observed in their sister group, indicating that this might correspond to a specialization exclusive for TRPV channels.
source: Although the residues in TRPA1 are still in close contact, they do not form the compact stacking observed in their sister group, indicating that this might correspond to a specialization exclusive for TRPV channels (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4b and c, with an inference about specialization.

claim: crTRP1 does not clearly form a compact-extended AC.
source: In contrast to these examples, crTRP1 does not clearly form a compact-extended AC.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: The presence of conserved aromatics next to ligand-binding sites, or even forming part of them, suggests a mechanism in which the AC acts by imparting rigidity to the region and functionally linking the transmembrane helices 1–4, facilitating the translation of mechanical force from the ligand-binding sites to the CDs that connect multiple parts of the channel including the TDh, cytoplasmic CD, and pre-TM1.
source: The presence of these conserved aromatics next to ligand-binding sites, or even forming part of them, suggests a mechanism in which the AC acts by imparting rigidity to the region and functionally linking the transmembrane helices 1–4, facilitating the translation of mechanical force from the ligand-binding sites to the CDs that connect multiple parts of the channel including the TDh, cytoplasmic CD, and pre-TM1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations.

claim: Large variability in the distances between residues located within the TM1–TM4 region was observed.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed a large variability in the distances between residues located within the TM1–TM4 region (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Minimal or no change in mean distance was observed among the conserved aromatics.
source: However, minimal or no change in mean distance was observed among the conserved aromatics (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: The role of the conserved aromatics might not be related to being part of a switch but rather stitching channel machinery in place.
source: This suggests to us that their role might not be related to being part of a switch but rather stitching channel machinery in place.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distance matrix analysis results.

claim: The connectivity and association between amino acids in the TM1-TM4 region has been shaped differently in the most represented subfamilies (TRPV, TRPM, and TRPC).
source: The analysis of the most represented subfamilies (TRPV, TRPM, and TRPC) shows that the connectivity and association between amino acids in this region has been shaped differently (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c-h).
evidence: This is a result from the distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c-h.

claim: Sequence and structure-based analyses support the notion of progressive structural transitions enabling the functional specialization of the LBD within each different subfamily.
source: Considering the role of the region in ligand binding, our sequence and structure-based analyses support the notion of progressive structural transitions enabling the functional specialization of the LBD within each different subfamily.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequence and structural analysis results.

claim: The presence of a group of three aromatics facing inside the VSLD is conserved in TPC's domain 1 and absent in domain 2 that is devoid of an extended aromatic network, resembling Nav channels.
source: Finally, consistent with the notion that TPC channels are close relatives of the TRP family, the presence of a group of three aromatics facing inside the VSLD is conserved in TPC's domain 1 and absent in domain 2 that is devoid of an extended aromatic network, resembling Nav channels (analyzed on mTPC1, PDB:6C96; NaV1.4, PDB:6AGF).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis of TPC channels.

claim: Unlike for TRPs, the AC in TPC channels looks less cohesive, or 'disconnected'.
source: Unlike for TRPs, the AC in TPC channels looks less cohesive, or 'disconnected' (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: TRP channels show a domain-swapped configuration.
source: TRP channels show a domain-swapped configuration (Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The VSLD/LBD of one subunit appears in close contact with its pore domain (PD) through the protein backbone and, at the same time, in close contact with the PD of the neighboring subunit.
source: That is, the VSLD/LBD of one subunit appears in close contact with its pore domain (PD) through the protein backbone and, at the same time, in close contact with the PD of the neighboring subunit.
evidence: This represents established structural knowledge about TRP channels.

claim: A conserved interaction is formed by a residue at the middle of TM4 and a residue that is consistently preceding a signature residue in TM5 (Phe591 in rTRPV1).
source: By inspecting the structural data, we found a conserved interaction formed by a residue at the middle of TM4 and a residue that is consistently preceding a signature residue in TM5 (Phe591 in rTRPV1; Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Although the nature of the interaction varies, it is present in all surveyed structures.
source: Although the nature of the interaction varies, it is present in all surveyed structures (Figure 5b; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Such interaction would put in direct contact TM helices 4 and 5 from different subunits.
source: Such interaction would put in direct contact TM helices 4 and 5 from different subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the case of TRPV channels, this interaction might support long-range communication between patches P1 and P2 from different subunits via the aromatics running alongside the LBD.
source: For the case of TRPV channels, this interaction might support long-range communication between patches P1 and P2 from different subunits via the aromatics running alongside the LBD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis.

claim: Such putative connection would be absent in subfamilies not presenting a stacked arrangement such as TRPC.
source: Such putative connection would be absent in subfamilies not presenting a stacked arrangement such as TRPC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The high conservation of these residues and their relative positions within the structure suggests a common mechanism in TRPs where the selectivity filter (P2) would be functionally connected to the ligand-binding site located on a neighboring transmembrane region.
source: The high conservation of these residues and their relative positions within the structure suggests a common mechanism in TRPs where the selectivity filter (P2) would be functionally connected to the ligand-binding site located on a neighboring transmembrane region.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the sequence and structural analysis.

claim: The PKD2/MCLN clade was recovered sister to all other TRP lineages.
source: Similar to other studies, we recovered the PKD2/MCLN clade sister to all other TRP lineages (Montell, 2005; Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007; Kozma et al., 2018); however, it is different from the proposed scenario by Himmel et al., 2020 in which they suggest that the TRPY/TRPF clade could belong to the group that includes PKD2 and MCLN.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The phylogenetic arrangement differs from the proposed scenario by Himmel et al., 2020 in which they suggest that the TRPY/TRPF clade could belong to the group that includes PKD2 and MCLN.
source: Similar to other studies, we recovered the PKD2/MCLN clade sister to all other TRP lineages (Montell, 2005; Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007; Kozma et al., 2018); however, it is different from the proposed scenario by Himmel et al., 2020 in which they suggest that the TRPY/TRPF clade could belong to the group that includes PKD2 and MCLN.
evidence: This is a comparison of the phylogenetic results with previous literature.

claim: TRP channel's ability to respond to temperature is a property that has been reported in 11 TRP channels TRPV1–4, TRPA1, TRPM2, TRPM3, TRPM4, TRPM5, TRPM8, and TRPC5.
source: TRP channel's ability to respond to temperature is a property that has been reported in 11 TRP channels TRPV1–4, TRPA1, TRPM2, TRPM3, TRPM4, TRPM5, TRPM8, and TRPC5 (Caterina et al., 1997; Saito and Shingai, 2006; Saito et al., 2011; Ferreira et al., 2015; Saito and Tominaga, 2015; Castillo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The phenotype distribution suggests a scenario involving multiple gain and/or losses of the ability to respond to temperature.
source: Considering the phylogenetic relationships among TRPs, the phenotype distribution suggests a scenario involving multiple gain and/or losses of the ability to respond to temperature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis and known phenotypes.

claim: The temperature-sensitive crTRP1 from the unicellular algae C. reinhardtii shares a common ancestor with the TRPM subfamily, that includes at least five out of eight members displaying different degrees of temperature sensitivity.
source: The temperature-sensitive crTRP1 (Arias-Darraz et al., 2015; McGoldrick et al., 2019), from the unicellular algae C. reinhardtii, shares a common ancestor with the TRPM subfamily, that includes at least five out of eight members displaying different degrees of temperature sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis and previous literature on temperature sensitivity.

claim: Temperature-dependent gating is apparently lost in TRPCs, with the notable exception of TRPC5.
source: The feature is apparently lost in TRPCs, with the notable exception of TRPC5 (Zimmermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis and previous literature, with citation.

claim: Temperature-dependent gating is strongly conserved in the TRPV group, with the exception of calcium-selective TRPV5 and TRPV6.
source: In contrast, temperature-dependent gating is strongly conserved in the TRPV group, with the exception of calcium-selective TRPV5 and TRPV6.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis and known phenotypes.

claim: The phenotype of temperature sensitivity was apparently preserved in TRPA1 during a process of specialization that involved multiple sequence changes in the so called 'allosteric nexus' region, while preserving the core structural features defining GI-TRP channels.
source: The phenotype was apparently preserved in TRPA1 during a process of specialization that involved multiple sequence changes in the so called 'allosteric nexus' region (Paulsen et al., 2015), while preserving the core structural features defining GI-TRP channels presented in here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic and structural analysis, with citation to previous literature.

claim: Recent structural work, anisotropic thermal diffusion calculations, and a combination of patch clamp fluorometry, mutagenesis, and molecular modeling suggest that the temperature-dependent transition may initiate close to the intracellular water-lipid boundary and propagate through a conformational wave.
source: Recent structural work (Nadezhdin et al., 2021b; Kwon et al., 2021), anisotropic thermal diffusion calculations (Diaz-Franulic et al., 2016), and a combination of patch clamp fluorometry, mutagenesis, and molecular modeling (Yang et al., 2018) suggest that the temperature-dependent transition may initiate close to the intracellular water-lipid boundary and propagate through a conformational wave.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: This collective molecular motion is enabled by a network of interactions involving fingerprint residues Trp426 and Phe434, which connect to the transmembrane helices via the AC and the TM4–TM5 linker/TDh interface.
source: Interestingly, this collective molecular motion is enabled by a network of interactions involving fingerprint residues Trp426 and Phe434, which connect to the transmembrane helices via the AC and the TM4–TM5 linker/TDh interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis and previous literature.

claim: The conserved residues and interactions highlighted in the present work suggest new and exciting mutagenesis experiments that could potentially dissect the temperature-driven conformational wave and thus shed light on the microscopic mechanism of heat activation.
source: The conserved residues and interactions highlighted in the present work suggest new and exciting mutagenesis experiments that could potentially dissect the temperature-driven conformational wave and thus shed light on the microscopic mechanism of heat activation.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions based on the findings.
